newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil sugar producers request zero export tax.
newsitem.headline: Brazil sugar producers request zero export tax.

text.p: Brazilian sugar producers Wednesday were sending an official request to the Industry and Commerce and Finance Ministers that the government cut an export tax on all sugar to zero, a producer official said.
Under the current crop plan, Brazilian producers can export 5.39 million tonnes of sugar, divided up into individual quotas, with a zero export tax.
But any excess exports are liable to a 40 percent tax unless producers negotiate with the government for additional quotas.
Today's request follows a meeting Tuesday between producing officials and Industry and Commerce Minister Francisco Dornelles to discuss the issue, the official said.
"The minister wanted to liberate further quotas. But we said that we wanted a zero export tax immediately," the producer official said.
The Finance Ministry has already indicated it accepts a zero export tax on sugar as part of a gradual process to open up the country's sugar and alcohol sector, he added.
Previously Industry and Commerce Ministry officials have said they support the idea of freeing sugar exports but only as of the start of the next crop year in May 1998.
The request is expected to be analysed at a regular meeting of Central Bank officials held every Wednesday.
A government official said it was very likely that the issue could be decided at the next meeting to be held on July 16.

The producer official estimated that with a zero export tax on all sugar exports, Brazil overseas shipments could reach 6.4 million tonnes in 1997/98 (May/April) or around one million tonnes more than included in the current crop plan.
But much would depend on demand on the international market, he added.

The zero tax would effectively mean that the individual sugar export quotas allocated to producers would no longer be relevant and that producers would only be committed to meeting government-set targets for alcohol production and supply of sugar to the domestic market.

By retaining the export tax albeit at zero, the government on the other hand still would have the power to introduce a higher tax to slow down sugar exports if it fears that internal supply of sugar and alcohol are being compromised.
